claims.text: Kaplan et al. (2020) reported α=0.73, β=0.27 (models should scale 4.7× larger than data) while Chinchilla (2022) found α≈0.50, β≈0.50 (equal scaling). Later re-analysis by Epoch AI (2024) and Farseer (2025) identified that Kaplan measured loss during training on early tokens before context saturation, excluded embedding parameters, and used fixed learning rate schedules not tailored to model size. When these papers standardized on full-context evaluation and total parameter accounting, they converged on Chinchilla's exponents. Prior 'conflicting' scaling laws were optimizing different objectives.

claims.text: The Chinchilla parametric loss function decomposes loss into separate capacity bottleneck (A/N^α, where α≈0.34) and data bottleneck (B/D^β, where β≈0.28) terms. Since α > β, capacity diminishing returns decay slower than data returns, meaning you typically exhaust data diversity before exhausting model capacity. By sweeping model size at fixed compute (IsoFLOP methodology), you observe a U-shaped loss curve whose shape indicates which bottleneck dominates—allowing you to choose whether your next budget increase should fund more training tokens or a larger model.
